title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side.

title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply.

title: Daubert-Ready Sample Audits for Litigation Surveys
one_liner: A neutral data-quality auditor that gives survey experts and litigators a signed, control-calibrated audit of the respondent sample behind a Lanham Act, false-advertising or damages survey, or a teardown of the other side's sample.
customer: Wedge: the 30-60 US testifying survey experts and boutique survey-litigation consultancies who field likelihood-of-confusion, secondary-meaning, deception and conjoint-damages surveys, plus the IP and false-advertising litigation partners who retain them. Later: in-house counsel at CPG and pharma companies that run claim-substantiation surveys for FTC or NAD challenges.
problem: A litigation survey is only worth what survives cross-examination and a Rule 702 challenge. Until recently 'we removed speeders and failed attention checks' was an adequate answer on sample quality. Agents now pass those checks (99.8% of 6,000 trials in the parent's evidence), so the standard defence is hollow. Opposing experts can attack the panel, and the amended Rule 702 (Dec 2023) makes the proponent show reliability by a preponderance. Survey experts have no neutral way to show their sample is clean, and rebuttal experts have no fast, credible way to quantify contamination in the other side's produced respondent data. The fee is small next to the $50k-$300k+ a litigation survey costs (from background knowledge, to be verified in calls) and the case value behind it.
solution: Two case-driven products. (1) Proponent audit: before full fielding, insert canary and honeypot items (with the expert's sign-off) and run a pilot. Ingest detection signals licensed from dtect, Verisoul or DQC rather than building an ensemble. Field the test and control cells on a 150-300-complete slice of a licensed address-recruited panel (NORC, Ipsos or Verasight-style, resold, not built). Deliver contamination-adjusted net-effect estimates with bounds, a sensitivity table ('conclusion holds up to X% contamination') and a hash-timestamped chain-of-custody field log. A named academic methodologist signs a declaration that can be attached to the expert report. (2) Rebuttal teardown: a fixed-scope 10-business-day analysis of the opposing side's produced respondent-level data, built to fit rebuttal-report deadlines. The firm never opines on the merits (confusion, deception, damages). It only certifies or attacks data quality, so it is a supplier to every expert rather than a competitor.
why_now: Agents that pass attention checks (2025-26) killed the old defence. Pew's Aug 2026 finding of 18% bogus respondents in opt-in samples, with trap questions and Sentry disagreeing on who is bogus, gives opposing counsel a citable, public source. The Dec 2023 Rule 702 amendment gives judges an explicit mandate to scrutinise reliability. The first contested Daubert motion where an expert cannot rebut agent contamination will spread fast through the small survey-expert community.
revenue_model: $12-40k per case engagement (proponent audit or rebuttal teardown), billed to the law firm as consulting-expert cost and passed through to the client. $60-120k/yr retainers for survey-expert firms that run 8-15 surveys a year, covering unlimited pilots and field-log stamps. $2-5k per survey for a hash-stamped field log as a low-touch add-on. Later, a $25-50k/yr library subscription for in-house claim-substantiation teams. Gross margin is mostly the licensed control slice (about $3-8k per engagement) plus methodologist hours.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not paying for truth. The buyer is paying, with the client's litigation budget, for insurance against cross-examination, so willingness to pay is set by case value and not by the $/complete price that caps every other idea in this space. The test-versus-control design used in litigation surveys also means random-answering bots hit both cells and pull net confusion toward zero. Contamination therefore tends to hurt plaintiffs and help defendants, so both sides have a reason to buy: proponents to insulate, opponents to attack. Once a court admits or credits the method, it becomes citable precedent. That is process power and switching cost that no detection API can copy.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every survey expert named in published Lanham Act opinions of the last five years and 40 IP litigation partners. Run 10 price-validation calls (5 experts, 5 partners) and stop if fewer than 4 say $15k+ is reasonable. Days 10-25: buy about 300 completes each from 4 panel vendors on a classic Eveready-format and Teflon-format design, plus a 150-complete control slice from a licensed address-recruited panel. Measure how many bots it takes to swing net confusion by 5 points. Days 20-30: publish 'How many agents does it take to flip a confusion survey?' as a white paper and CLE talk proposal. Offer two free rebuttal teardowns on public-record survey data in exchange for permission to cite. Sign one academic survey methodologist as chief methodologist and testifier.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection vendors (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, ReDem, CleanID) sell entry-time filtering to panels at cents per complete and produce nothing a court can use. They are input suppliers here. Data Quality Co-op's scorecard and Data Trust Score describe suppliers in general and do not give a case-specific, testifiable declaration. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample, so opposing counsel would call it conflicted. Pew and NORC publish the methodology for free but not per case, and not in expert-report form. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the self-grading problem that Daubert challenges target. Existing litigation-survey consultancies field surveys and testify on merits, so they are customers, not rivals.

title: Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring
one_liner: Drivers upload settlement stubs and AI turns them into the true, receipts-backed pay per mile and per hour away from home for every carrier, sold as a hiring credential and as income proof for lenders.
customer: Honest mid-size carriers (50 to 1,000 trucks) that pay $6k to $15k to hire each driver and can't prove their pay claims are real. Secondary buyers are mortgage and auto lenders (bank-statement and non-QM brokers) who serve drivers.
problem: Recruiter ads say 'up to 75 cents a mile, $100k+' but realized pay is often 20 to 35% lower after unpaid or practical-versus-paid miles, unpaid detention, chargebacks and deductions. Driver turnover at big truckload carriers runs near 90%, and job ads are so discredited that honest carriers can't stand out. Drivers whose pay is structured as tax-free 'per diem' also see a low W-2 and get denied mortgages after 20 years of work. Estimates say the English-proficiency and non-domiciled CDL crackdowns will pull 214,000 to 437,000 drivers (5 to 12% of CDL holders) from the supply over 2 to 3 years, so carriers are competing harder for domestic drivers.
solution: A mobile app where drivers photograph settlement stubs and pay statements. AI extracts paid miles, deadhead, detention, deductions, per diem and time away from home, and computes effective take-home per hour on the road, not just per mile. Public carrier pages show verified figures such as '312 verified drivers, median $0.61 per paid mile, $17.40 per hour away'. Carriers that look good pay for a 'Verified Pay' badge and applicant funnel. A second product builds an income-verification packet from stubs and deposit statements for lenders. Fraud controls include stub-format checks, duplicate detection and consistency with driver-reported miles.
why_now: Shrinking driver supply from the 2025 to 2026 English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement (proposed codification rule published Aug 10, 2026) and the Feb 2026 non-domiciled CDL restrictions means cost-per-hire is rising. Vision-model OCR of messy pay stubs is now cheap and accurate. Truth-in-leasing rules already require itemized settlements, so the raw material exists.
revenue_model: Carrier subscriptions of $500 to $3,000 a month for the verified page, analytics and applicant funnel. Lender referral fees of $300 to $1,000 per funded mortgage or truck loan. Free for drivers, which keeps the data supply growing.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers don't compare carriers by ads, they ask in the truck-stop lot 'what do you actually clear?' The only artifact they trust is a pay stub. The honest carriers are the ones locked out of trust, so they are the natural paying customer. The true unit of pay is dollars per hour away from home, because 14-hour clocks, detention and unpaid waiting eat the mileage math. And per-diem income structures are a hidden mortgage trap that a stub-based income packet can fix.
first_30_days: Post in trucker Facebook groups, Reddit and TikTok: 'Upload your stub, see your real rate vs. what your carrier advertised.' Aim for 500 stubs in 30 days. Publish a 'State of Real Pay' report ranking 20 named carriers and pitch it to trade press (Overdrive, CDLLife, FreightWaves). Sell 'Verified Pay' badges to the 5 mid-size fleets whose numbers look best, and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TruckersReport (carrier reviews and salary survey), Best Fleets to Drive For (CarriersEdge), Tenstreet (Driver Pulse, IntelliApp, Hiring Center), Drive My Way. White space: Web search was unavailable (the session's 200-search budget was used up), so this rests on about 25 direct page fetches plus prior knowledge. Confidence is moderate to low. A reviewer should re-run searches for 'verified driver pay', 'settlement stub scanner' and 'trucker mortgage per diem' before committing.

I found no product that does all of this: (1) collect settlement stubs, (2) verify them with fraud checks, and (3) publish per-carrier, receipts-backed effective pay, including dollars per hour away from home. The closest, TruckersReport, has an unverified self-reported salary survey run by a site paid by carriers' recruiting budgets. Best Fleets to Drive For is survey-based. Tenstreet and Drive My Way own recruiting flow but show no pay-verification product.

Specific unserved gaps:
- A trust-backed pay number that uses stubs as proof, computed as dollars per hour on the road rather than per mile.
- Lease-purchase and owner-operator drivers, whose settlements are itemized and who are the most exposed to deceptive ads.
- A stub-based income packet that handles per-diem structures for non-QM and bank-statement lenders. Truv and Argyle verify through payroll connections and are not built for per-diem trucker income.

Weak points that could still sink it:
1. Cold start and selection bias. Unhappy drivers upload more, and carriers with a bad median will not buy a badge. A pay-for-badge model also has a credibility conflict.
2. Stubs do not show time away from home. Hours-away metrics need driver-entered dates or ELD integration, which is hard.
3. The truth-in-leasing itemized-settlement rule (49 CFR 376.12) applies to owner-operator leases, not W-2 company drivers. The idea's 'raw material already exists' claim is only partly true. I could not fetch the regulation this session.
4. Publishing rankings of named carriers invites legal threats. Self-published analytics are not covered by Section 230 the way user reviews are.
5. Per-funded-loan referral fees to a non-lender may run into RESPA Section 8, so this needs counsel. Lenders will also likely re-verify borrower-supplied stubs, which limits the lender product's value. This is from prior knowledge and not verified.

title: Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay
one_liner: A price-sheet-plus-gauss-meter program that pays scrapyards for magnet-dense motors and rotors they currently sell as steel and copper.
customer: Rare-earth magnet recyclers and magnet makers needing domestic recycled feed (they pay per kg with assay). Scrapyards, motor rebuilders and appliance/HVAC recyclers are the sellers.
problem: The rare-earth bottleneck is 'collection and disassembly rather than recovery chemistry.' Hard-drive magnet removal often costs more than the material is worth. Yards sell EV drive units, servo and elevator motors, and e-bike hub motors by copper and steel weight, and the NdFeB rotors go into the steel shred.
solution: Skip HDDs and target a short list of heavy, magnet-dense items. Yards get a phone app plus a $150 gauss meter that identifies magnet-bearing units and shows a payout per unit or per rotor. A mobile pull cell or the yard's own labor removes rotors. We aggregate and assay them, then sell a certified, traceable magnet-feed stream to recyclers.
why_now: The IEA puts China at about 90% of material recovery capacity. The DoD-MP deal and the Texas magnet campus create domestic pull, and DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026. Recyclers such as Cyclic Materials and IonicRE are funded and need feed.
revenue_model: Spread between the recycler's price per kg of assayed magnet feed and the yard payout plus pull cost. Optional premium for defense-traceable lots. Small SaaS fee for the identification and price app.
non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth economics fail on tiny magnets (HDDs) but work on a few heavy items. No one publishes a price by motor model, so yards do not know a rotor holds hundreds of grams to kilograms of NdFeB. Price discovery is the missing product, not a new chemistry.
first_30_days: Buy 5 gauss meters. Visit 10 auto shredders and motor shops and measure and photograph 200 units. Build a price sheet by model. Get an offtake LOI from one magnet recycler that needs feed. Pay 3 yards on the first 50 units and publish the results to recruit more.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Cyclic Materials, HyProMag USA (CoTec / Mkango JV), ERI (Electronics Recyclers International), Noveon Magnetics. White space: Evidence caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran zero successful web searches and relied on direct page fetches of about 20 company and source URLs. Several were 404, 503 or blocked. Coverage of forums, RFPs, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and open-source tools is therefore missing. Treat this as a partial check, not a clean bill of health.

What remains unserved, judged from the company pages I could read:
(1) A yard-facing price and identification product. No fetched page (Cyclic, HyProMag, ReElement, Ionic, Noveon) publishes a payout by motor make and model, a magnet-mass lookup, or a handheld gauss-meter workflow for yard staff. Cyclic's supplier page explicitly gives no pricing, logistics or ID tools ('contact us to get started').
(2) The long tail of small and mid-size auto shredders, motor rebuilders, elevator and industrial motor shops, and e-bike hub-motor scrap. ERI is anchored on e-waste and the OEM/ITAD channel, and Cyclic's named categories are drive motors, HDDs, robotics, defense and wind. Elevator, servo and e-bike hub motors are not named.
(3) Chain-of-custody and assay data for defense-traceable lots.

Where the idea is weak: the buyers are building their own procurement. Cyclic takes whole units without dismantling, so the 'mobile pull cell' adds little. Cyclic and HyProMag have stated supply pipelines and can capture the aggregator margin by paying yards directly once yards know what they hold. The spread-based aggregator model is exposed to that squeeze. The durable wedge is the data and identification layer.

title: Hall-Ready Gate for Liquid-Cooled GPU Tranches
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day release/hold decision, made 60-90 days before GPU delivery, on whether a liquid-cooled data hall will be energized and flowing when the racks arrive.
customer: Credit-desk principals and VPs at mid-market private credit funds, BDCs and specialty lenders on their first to fifth delayed-draw GPU facility to a sub-investment-grade neocloud, with no in-house commissioning bench. Secondary: mid-size AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity in a non-hyperscale hall. Excluded on purpose: hyperscalers and mega-funds that have their own engineers.
problem: In a delayed-draw GPU facility, the lender funds a GPU purchase order on the sponsor's word that the hall will be ready. That is roughly $3M+ per NVL72-class rack and hundreds of racks per hall. If the hall slips, the GPUs idle. My estimate is about $0.75M per day per $1B stranded (8% interest plus 5-year straight-line depreciation). Nobody on the lender's side is retained to say 'hold' at that moment. IEs certify construction draws. The technical advisors seen in GPU deals check fleet files, telemetry and power documents (per Peony). The RFS date is a sponsor sales number. NVL72-class racks have no air-cooled fallback, so the loop must be proven flushed, filled and leak-tested before any tray draws power. That work is done last, by scarce people. The parent's weakness was a broad 'better IE' pitch, sold through trust-gated relationships, with no software moat and an unproven right of site access. All of these are addressed below.
solution: One product for one decision, the 'Gate Memo'. It is $30K fixed, delivered in 10 business days. It has 12 binary hold-point tests, all in the failure zone: (1) written utility authorization to energize; (2) MV gear energized, with serials matched to bills of lading; (3) Cx Level 4 closed, with Level 5 IST script pass/fail counts; (4) CDU flush and pressure-test logs signed by the mechanical contractor; (5) punch-list burn-down slope over the last three weekly snapshots; (6) OEM startup technicians booked for named dates; (7) fiber acceptance; and five others. It also includes one site day by an ex-Cx lead and a probability of RFS by the sponsor's date. The memo ends in one of three recommendations: release, release with staged delivery, or hold N weeks. It is expressly not a certification. It does no draw certification, no cost-to-complete and no liability-bearing sign-off, and it leaves those to the IE. That keeps liability small and stops us from being an IE substitute. Access is solved with a free 'Readiness Rider', a two-page information-covenant and hold-point rider that finance counsel can paste into GPU facility documents. It gives the lender the evidence pack and one site visit as a condition precedent to each GPU tranche. The rider is both the access mechanism and the lead generator. After the gate, a $6K/month watch runs until RFS.
why_now: GPU-backed delayed-draw loans became standardized and large in 2026 (for example CoreWeave's $8.5B A3-rated DDTL closed 2026-03-31). That is pulling in mid-market credit funds that copy the structure without an infrastructure bench. Liquid-cooled racks removed the air-cooled fallback. Liquid-cooling engineers top a Q2 2026 US bottleneck index (Spencer Ogden, scarcity 80/100), and one missing controls technician can hold a finished hall out of service. Lenders are capping neocloud exposure and neocloud deals are stalling on credit risk. Satellite vendors have commoditized the exterior view, so the interior last 90 days is the scarce truth.
revenue_model: $30K per Gate Memo and $6K/month per hall for the watch. A retainer of $75K per fund buys 3 gates. Delivery cost is a 1099 Cx lead for about 4 desk days plus 1 site day, roughly $8-10K, so gross margin is about 65-70%. Year-1 target is 25 gates ($750K) plus watch fees ($250-300K), with about 6 principals doing the work. Year 2 adds a licensed benchmark dataset.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not purchasing a forecast. The buyer is purchasing an option trigger. The gate is timed to a decision with a cheap 'hold' branch (staged delivery or a 2-4 week deferral) and an expensive 'release' branch (idle carry). A false alarm costs weeks and a miss costs months of carry, so a forecast that is only about 65% accurate still has large positive value. This is why the lender does not need certainty and why the fee is trivially small next to the decision. Second, every gate produces structured data that IEs, who bill hourly and file Word reports, never accumulate: punch-list burn-down slope by hall, OEM startup lead times, and utility energization durations. After roughly 30 gates that becomes a reference-class dataset that sharpens each forecast, which is a process and data moat built from work you were being paid to do anyway.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign 4 retired or between-jobs Cx leads on 1099 contracts, prioritizing anyone who has commissioned liquid-cooled GB-class halls. Draft the 12-test Gate Memo template. Run it retroactively on 2 publicly delayed projects and publish the teardowns. Week 2: give 2 boutique finance law firms that do GPU facilities a co-branded Readiness Rider. List 40 mid-market credit funds with GPU or data center facilities, sourced from DDTL closing press releases and BDC filings. Weeks 3-4: hold 25 conversations with principals and VPs. Offer a design-partner Gate Memo at $15K on a live deal in exchange for an anonymized case study and permission to keep anonymized metrics. Target 2 signed by day 30. Riskiest assumption to test first: a credit desk will pay $30K for a hold/release memo that is not a certification. Test it with a pre-sale at day 14.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. | How this version avoids them: Traditional IEs: my search confirmed Sargent & Lundy markets data center owner's engineering, commissioning and performance-test oversight, and IE due diligence for lenders and investors, so this is a real incumbent. We do not compete for the IE mandate. We sell a 10-day fixed-price hold decision on one window, take no certification liability, and can sit beside the IE. Their hourly, multi-month, borrower-paid economics plausibly conflict with a small buyer-side product (hypothesis, unverified). SynMax/IIR/Epoch/Currence: their exterior and desk data are ingested as inputs and stop before energization and commissioning. SemiAnalysis: covers neocloud credit, pricing and operations, not hall-level readiness, and we do not touch GPU pricing. Peony-described GPU technical advisors: scope is fleet file, telemetry and power documents, so we own the pre-energization window. Watch for scope creep by them. Uptime Tier Certification: an end-of-build certificate, not a schedule decision. The narrow wedge (liquid-cooled halls, non-hyperscale sponsors, mid-market lenders) is also where large IEs' pricing and minimum engagement sizes fit worst.

title: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates
one_liner: An adequacy auditor that scores any carrier-side smoke, ash and soot report against a public, versioned sampling grid. It then drafts the AB 1795 deficiency letter and supplemental sampling plan, and sells to public adjusters and plaintiff attorneys in the Eaton and Palisades zones.
customer: Wedge: 15-25 licensed public adjuster firms working standing-home smoke claims in Altadena, Pasadena, Pacific Palisades and Malibu, plus 3-5 plaintiff firms running the Ghazarian-style class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors. Later: homeowners buying direct at about $295, then carrier claims-legal teams running pre-flight audits on their own vendors.
problem: Every standing-home claimant holds a carrier-vendor IH report saying 'clean' or 'minor'. Neither the public adjuster nor the attorney can tell quickly whether it was under-sampled. Carrier-retained hygienists reportedly take about 10 samples in 3,000 sq ft, skip attics, wall cavities and HVAC, and compare results to urban background dust. A CIH second opinion costs $2k-$4k+ and takes weeks from a scarce pool. Purdue's free review is capacity-limited and does not produce claim-ready output. From Jan 1, 2027 AB 1795 makes insurers pay for testing that is 'necessary', but only if someone shows what is necessary and missing.
solution: Upload the IH report and lab PDF. LLM extraction with human QA pulls sample count, locations, media (wipe, tape lift, air, bulk), comparison basis, detection limits and skipped zones. It scores them against a public 'Adequacy Grid' built from AIHA's wildfire guide, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, 40 CFR 745.227 and 8 CCR 1529, with every criterion cited. Within 48 hours the customer gets a 2-page scorecard listing what was not sampled, a statute-cited deficiency letter for the PA or attorney to send, and a supplemental sampling plan that a partner CIH-of-record can sign, with a priced quote from a partner testing firm. The plaintiff tier ingests hundreds of reports in batch for pattern analytics (share with zero attic samples, samples per 1,000 sq ft by vendor). The grid is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC publishes standards in 2028-29. We do not sample, employ technicians, or give expert opinions.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a 30-day inspection duty and a duty to pay for necessary testing, and it presumes smoke, ash and soot in a standing home came from the fire. Class actions over vendor sampling were filed in Feb 2026, LA County sued State Farm on 8/31/2026, and 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage are in play. Cheap LLM document extraction makes a 48-hour, hundreds-of-dollars audit feasible where it used to be a $3k CIH engagement.
revenue_model: Public adjusters pay $395 per audit, or $2,500 a month for up to 10 active files. The CIH-signed supplemental sampling plan costs $900, split 50/50 with the partner CIH. Plaintiff-firm pattern analytics run $40k-$150k per engagement, for example a 300-report batch. The partner testing firm pays a flat referral fee on supplemental sampling it wins, or we take none if that raises fee-splitting concerns. Phase 2 sells carrier claims-legal teams a $2k-$5k per-vendor-report pre-flight audit. Bottom-up: even 15% of 13,000 homes at $395 plus a few analytics contracts is about $1.5M-$2.5M in year one, so the wedge is small and the dataset is the asset.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of leverage is the omission list, not the test result. AB 1795 obliges the insurer to pay for necessary testing, and a scored list of what was not sampled and why it matters converts a fuzzy fight into a checklist the adjuster must answer in writing. Every audit also writes one structured row (vendor, square footage, samples, comparator, zones skipped), so the tool quietly builds the largest labeled dataset of how carrier vendors sample. Counter-positioning is real: HygieneTech, Rimkus and Safeguard cannot sell a tool that indicts carrier-side sampling without alienating their own clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: collect 25 real IH reports with consent from EFRU volunteers, two public adjusters and one attorney. Sign two CIHs at about $150/hr to review the rubric, and a toxicologist as advisor. Weeks 2-3: build Grid v0.1 as a spreadsheet plus extraction pipeline, targeting over 90% field-level accuracy on the 25 reports. Run free 48-hour audits for 10 PA files. Track whether the deficiency letter gets the carrier or FAIR Plan to authorize additional testing. Week 4: start charging $395 from audit #11, aiming for 30 paid audits and one attorney LOI for a 100-report batch pilot at about $25k. Before day 15, confirm from the chaptered AB 1795 text that there is no qualified-person or licensure rule that blocks a non-CIH from drafting a sampling plan for CIH signature.
lineage: mutation of I0715 ('Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup, EHS Analytical, Home BioTesting and Vert-type shops all sell sampling supply and are either carrier-conflicted or capacity-bound. We sell no sampling, so EHS and Home BioTesting become the partners who fulfil the supplemental plans and gain lead flow. Purdue's free review is bounded by grad-student capacity and has no claim-language deliverable, SLA or batch mode; we cite its method and offer a data-share and donation instead of competing. IICRC, AIHA and EFRU publish guidance and maps but sell no per-claim operational tool, so we build on them and ask EFRU for a data partnership. Safeguard's 'defensible framework' is a carrier-side essay, whereas ours is a scoring engine aimed at the policyholder side. State standards in 2028-29 change the grid's contents but not the need for an audit tool, so the business survives the standard rather than dying with it.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors.

title: Contingency Recovery for Contaminated Survey Sample
one_liner: A freight-audit-style recovery firm that finds contaminated and duplicated completes in the survey sample buyers already paid for, files credit claims against panel vendors, and keeps 25-35% of what it recovers.
customer: Wedge: mid-size full-service market research agencies (about 100-500 staff) that buy $1-10M a year of third-party online sample on fixed-fee client projects and absorb the reruns. Second wave: procurement teams at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms that already run recovery audits on freight, telecom and cloud spend but have never applied one to research sample.
problem: The parent idea asks insights teams to pay for a quality audit, and the research found no evidence anyone will pay $3-15k for one. Buyers do pay for money back. Kantar says post-field reconciliation (rejected sample) rates are up about 300% in three years, with some clients rejecting up to 40% of data (a vendor source). Contaminated completes that pass screening are paid for and used. The same panelist or device is also resold through several exchanges, so buyers pay twice for one human. Agencies eat the rerun cost, procurement never sees data quality, and nobody has respondent-level evidence strong enough to make a vendor pay. Vendors also fight individual rejections because their detector disagrees with the buyer's.
solution: Zero-upfront retrospective audit. The buyer gives read access to 12-24 months of respondent-level files, vendor IDs, invoices and MSAs. The firm runs LLM-assisted open-end forensics, cross-vendor duplicate detection (hashed device, IP and open-end similarity) and paradata review. It ingests detection flags from dtect, Verisoul or DQC where the buyer already has them. A 300-500-complete verified-human control cell per major vendor calibrates a population-level contamination estimate with error bounds. The firm then files claims for replacement completes, credits or refunds, citing the contractual quality clause. Claims argue that a vendor's batch exceeded the SLA (e.g. above 5% invalid, 95% CI) rather than fighting each flagged complete, which is where vendors dispute. Fee is 25-35% of value recovered, with no recovery meaning no fee. Stage two is prospective: a payment-hold or escrow layer where vendor payment for a batch releases after a control-calibrated pass, and a monitoring subscription.
why_now: Agents passing attention checks mean the largest share of contamination is now undetected at entry, which is exactly the paid-for-but-invalid pool that recovery targets. The cost stack collapsed: reading 10 million open-ended answers used to need human coders at dollars per complete, and LLMs now do it at fractions of a cent, so a contingency model works even on mid-size invoices. Pew's Aug 2026 study and NORC's fraud review give claim letters a public, credible methodology to cite. Buyers are already 'auditing suppliers, bringing sampling in-house and demanding accountability' (Greenbook), so procurement is primed.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25-35% of recovered value. Illustrative unit economics, which are assumptions to test: $3M annual sample spend, 5-10% recoverable ($150-300k), 50% recovered, 30% fee, so $22-45k per customer per year. That is lower than the parent's $50-150k programmes but has almost no sales friction. Add-ons are a prospective monitoring subscription ($2-4k/month) and escrow at 1-2% of sample spend. Roughly 150-250 agencies and 30-60 enterprise buyers as a bottom-up serviceable market gives a $10M+ ARR business without ever selling 'quality' as a line item.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody budgets for data quality, but everyone has a process for accounts receivable. Turning 'is my sample clean?' into 'how much money are we owed?' moves the buyer from the insights head, who has no budget and no pain, to finance and procurement, who have both. The scarce asset is the same verified-human reference as in the parent, but used differently. It is needed only in small doses (a few hundred humans per vendor), which removes the 2,000-person panel problem and lets it be licensed instead of built. Population-level SLA claims also sidestep the detector-disagreement fight that makes per-complete rejections so contentious.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: post to insights and procurement communities and DM 20 agency founders and heads of ops. The offer is 'send one vendor's last quarter of respondent files, we tell you the recoverable amount, you pay nothing unless we recover'. Days 5-15: have a contract lawyer review 10 sample sample-vendor MSAs and SOWs to extract quality, replacement and dispute clauses, and draft a standard claim letter. Days 10-25: build the pipeline (open-end similarity, hashed-device dedupe across vendors, control-cell comparison) and buy 300 completes each from 4 major vendors as baseline. Days 20-30: sign 3 contingency agreements and file the first claim. Success is the first $50k recovered by day 90. Kill if, after 5 audits, recoverable value is below 2% of spend or vendors refuse every claim.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection and scorecard vendors sell information or prevention: Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch Sentry, ReDem and CleanID filter at entry, and DQC sells supplier benchmarks and a trust score. None recovers money already paid, and all are cheap enough to be input suppliers rather than rivals. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the counterparty being claimed against, not a competitor. Verasight sells sample and could not credibly run claims against other vendors. The firm takes no referral fees from any vendor and never sells sample, so it stays neutral. Pew and NORC publish methodology free but never file claims. Traditional recovery-audit firms (freight, telecom, healthcare billing) do not touch survey sample, and the defensibility comes from the vendor-by-vendor claim-outcome database, which sets settlement rates and improves each claim.

title: Franchisee Flight Recorder and Recommendation Index
one_liner: Invert the advisor into a witness: a silent, tamper-evident ledger that records what the franchisor's AI recommended, what the owner ordered and what was binned, prices the gap under the owner's own contract, and scales into a franchisee-owned registry and a published Recommendation Cost Index for each chain.
customer: Start with legacy-contract Seven-Eleven owners in Kansai who fear OFC retaliation and will not use a tool that changes how they order. Then a franchisee-owned business cooperative, franchise-specialist law firms, lenders and analysts as data buyers, then regulators and convenience-store review panels as consumers of the aggregate. Later, Lawson and FamilyMart, Korea and Taiwan convenience chains, and other franchise systems with mandated promos, ordering or capex.
problem: The parent's insight stands: HQ recommendations optimize HQ's payoff. But advice tools stall on the owner's fear of the OFC, on HQ markdown pushes that commoditize the advice, and on Seven's new contract that shrinks the gap for new stores. Meanwhile owners have no evidence in the moments that matter: renewal or non-renewal talks, disputes about mismanagement, store sales, and any complaint to the JFTC or a METI panel. HQ holds the only record of what its AI recommended. The 2009 JFTC order on Seven-Eleven Japan and the Diamond and Toyo Keizai reporting show that regulators and press act on documented owner constraints, but individual owners hold anecdotes and one store is not statistics.
solution: Owner does nothing differently. Each day a LINE bot takes 3 photos or a forwarded CSV (the HQ order proposal screen, the order as placed, the disposal scan), extracts the data, and writes hashed records to a certified third-party time-stamp so the log is tamper-evident. The owner sees only a private monthly Ledger Statement: 'following HQ's proposals cost you X yen versus the optimum under your contract this month, Y yen cumulative', with no instruction and no OFC-visible change. The ledger is exported only on the owner's command to a lawyer, accountant, buyer or bank. Owners join a franchisee cooperative whose dues also fund a group-rate franchise-law retainer. Aggregated and anonymized across stores, the ledger yields per-item demand models that improve with store count and a quarterly Recommendation Cost Index for each chain, published as a neutral registry that regulators, lenders and press can cite. Every contract change (such as the 2027 Seven terms) becomes a natural experiment the index measures.
why_now: HQ AI ordering became the default at all three chains between 2023 and 2026, so a recorded 'recommended versus ordered versus binned' history now exists to capture. The disposal-share change in Seven's June 2026 contract shows HQ has conceded the conflict, and the METI convenience-store review panel is active. The 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka makes every wasted yen hurt more. Photo OCR and structured extraction make daily capture cost pennies, and certified time-stamping is standard infrastructure. The outcome of the 2023 union case (loss at the Supreme Court) shows that collective action needs a data and legal structure other than a labor union, which a cooperative can supply.
revenue_model: 1,980 yen per store per month from owners (about the price of consumer legal-expense insurance, an assumption to verify), with the cooperative dues bundled. Case packs for law firms at 300,000 to 500,000 yen with an expert declaration, optionally a contingency share where the law firm agrees. Annual data licenses to lenders, analysts and research bodies (roughly 3M to 10M yen each). At 15% of about 55,000 stores subscribing that is roughly 200M yen a year from owners alone, before case packs, licenses and other chains or countries. The registry and index are the longer-term standard-setting asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fear that blocks the advice product is the buying reason for the recorder. An owner who will never argue with the OFC will still pay a small fee for a private ledger he never has to show. The value is a network good: one owner's log is an anecdote, but thousands of timestamped logs are the only regulator-grade evidence that a franchisor's recommendations systematically diverge from franchisee payoff, and they cannot be replicated by anyone who lacks owner trust. Because it gives no advice it does not compete with HQ AI on accuracy and is immune to markdown-push commoditization, and it stays useful under any contract terms, including the 50/50 one where a gap remains (owner critical ratio about 36% versus HQ's about 70%).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the LINE bot and ledger on the founder's three stores (the first real evidence file) and commission a one-week franchise-lawyer memo on data ownership and confidentiality plus the business-cooperative structure. Days 10-30: pre-sell 30 owners at 1,980 yen per month for 12 months via Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups and 2 franchise-focused law firms, pitching it as 'a private record you never have to show anyone unless you need it'. Get one law firm to agree to a case-pack pilot price. Kill signals: fewer than 10 of 30 pre-sales, or the lawyer memo finds the HQ proposal screen cannot be recorded. Publish a one-page description of the Ledger Statement format and the planned index method to seed owner-to-owner sharing.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: 10x-or-inverted

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Verusen, SPARETECH GmbH, SAP (IBP, Store distribution) and IBM Maximo, Partium. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches of known companies. It is not a broad sweep. I could not run forum, Reddit, WhatsApp-group, RFP, Spanish/Portuguese-language or Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt searches. My 'nobody does cross-company mining pooling' finding is therefore unconfirmed and moderate-confidence.

STEP ONE (SAP dedupe and surplus cleaner) is crowded and should not be the business. Verusen has a live mining case study ($96.8M identified across 17 sites), a listing in the SAP Store, about $33M disclosed funding and enterprise references. SPARETECH does the same dedupe-and-surplus job. Partium and Syniti cover the normalization and SAP-cleansing pieces. The 'LLM cost collapsed, so now it's viable' argument is weak, because Verusen and SPARETECH already do this. The remaining wedge inside step one is small: mid-size mines (roughly $30-150M of spares, one SAP instance, no enterprise budget) below Verusen's Fortune-100 and multi-site-enterprise focus, sold on a success fee. That is a thin, copyable wedge.

STEP TWO (neutral, cross-operator critical-spares pool) is unserved among the players I checked. Verusen's sharing module is intra-company only and has no legal, insurance or inspection layer. Liquidity Services and RB Global sell surplus one-way and offer no loan or lease terms. Grid Assurance proves the pooled long-lead-spares subscription model for utilities, but nobody I found has applied it to mines. The unserved piece is the trust wrapper: a neutral entity, standard loan/lease agreement, third-party condition certification (vibration/NDT), logistics and insurance, and a single-point-of-failure spares register per district.

Risks I could not close out. (1) OEM reman, exchange and consignment programs (haul-truck components, mill liners, motors) are the real substitute for pooling. I could not verify their current terms because the Cat Reman fetch timed out. (2) Competition-law exposure when competing operators share inventory data needs early legal work. (3) The pooled-event frequency is low, so revenue per district is modest, and pooling in Chile or Peru needs local counsel. (4) Verusen could add an inter-company network cheaply; it already lists 'Spare Parts Sharing' and mining customers.

title: Delay-Risk Underwriting Desk for Data Center Insurers
one_liner: Sell Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters a 5-day hall-level readiness review and a portfolio 'collision calendar' so scarce DSU capacity can be written on more projects with fewer surprises, funded by the insured through a policy subjectivity, and later share in the premium.
customer: Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters and engineering leads at construction and specialty carriers and Lloyd's syndicates, plus the construction-broker teams that place data center DSU, and reinsurers. The insured (sponsor or lender-as-loss-payee) funds the work through a policy subjectivity. Later: backstop providers whose payout depends on delay thresholds, for example a backstop that only triggers if construction is under about 180 days late.
problem: DSU is the most contentious and expensive element of data center construction cover. Zurich commentary says adding it cuts available capacity, and underwriters call it disproportionate to premium. A flood of AI data center submissions is hampering underwriters' ability to process them, and DSU capacity is being reserved for projects judged best risk-managed. Delay exposure can exceed $1B on a single campus. Carriers now require phased handovers and detailed commissioning protocols, and they ask who is building, what equipment is specified and how commissioning sequences, but they can only check documents. DSU claims later need programme evidence, commissioning records and contemporaneous project records that are rarely captured cleanly. Worst, DSU losses are correlated through shared scarce pools (OEM startup crews, CDU and coolant-chemistry lots, utility energization windows) that per-risk underwriting cannot see.
solution: Four layers, sold in order. (1) Pre-bind 'DSU Readiness Review' in 5 business days per submission: desk review of the commissioning plan and sequence, capacity check of the contractor and OEM startup technicians, the utility energization path, a stage-appropriate Readiness Ladder score, and an underwriter-facing recommendation on deductible, waiting period and warranty wording. The underwriter commissions it and makes it a bind subjectivity, so the insured pays. (2) In-policy monthly Ladder monitoring, framed as compliance with the commissioning-protocol warranty, with early warnings to the underwriter. It also builds the contemporaneous evidence file for any delay notice, which cuts adjusting cost and disputes. (3) Portfolio 'Collision Calendar' for carriers and reinsurers: how many insured halls need the same OEM startup crew or utility window in the same month, so accumulation is priced rather than discovered. (4) Year 2: delegated authority. We become an MGA or coverholder on DSU excess layers, or offer a readiness-triggered parametric top-up where a verified Ladder milestone missed by a date is the trigger, earning a profit commission.
why_now: Insurers began rationing DSU exactly as data center project sizes jumped, with average project value rising from roughly $150M to roughly $3M+ per the coverage above. Aon expanded its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program to $2.5B in January 2026, covering construction all risks, DSU and operational damage/BI. Brokers publicly call DSU the pressure point. GPU-backed lenders and offtakers increasingly want delay cover as a condition of their deals, which pulls more submissions into an already constrained market. Document AI now turns commissioning scripts, test reports and punch lists into structured evidence for cents per page, so a small bench can serve many risks.
revenue_model: $12-25K per pre-bind review, paid by the insured through the subjectivity. $4-8K per month per policy for monitoring. $75-200K per year for carrier and reinsurer portfolio analytics. From year 2, a 10-20% profit commission on DSU premium written under delegated authority, which creates outcome-linked economics: we earn more when our screening keeps loss ratios low. Bottom-up: 40 reviewed risks and 25 monitored halls in year 1 is about $0.8-1.2M, before any delegated-authority income.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters do not buy diligence, they buy capacity. A credible hall-level score lets a carrier say yes to more DSU premium at the same loss ratio, so the buyer has a revenue reason to pay rather than a cost to minimize. Second, the pre-bind, in-policy and claims evidence needs are the same ledger, so one dataset serves three insurer budgets (underwriting, risk engineering, claims). Third, and most non-obvious, DSU is a systemic-correlation business disguised as a per-project one. Ten independently insured halls that all need the same OEM's startup crew in the same month are one risk, not ten. Nobody has the hall-level calendar to see it, and reinsurers will pay to.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 Cx leads plus one former DSU underwriter or claims adjuster as a paid adviser. Build a loss-cause taxonomy of about 6 delay causes from public litigation, insurer and broker commentary on delayed data center projects. Map about 20 DSU underwriters and construction-broker teams. Offer 8 of them a free shadow review, delivered in 5 days on a live submission with details blinded. Aim for 2 shadow reviews completed and 1 paid pilot by day 45. Insurance cycles are slow, so accept that. Riskiest assumption to test first: carriers will make an outside readiness review a subjectivity instead of relying on in-house or outsourced risk-engineering surveys. Ask each underwriter directly how surveys are commissioned today and who pays.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. This product is a different client and a different question, so there is no head-on IE bid. Satellite and database vendors (SynMax/IIR, Epoch, Currence): exterior or desk data, usable as inputs, with no commissioning evidence. SemiAnalysis: neocloud credit research, not insurance. Peony-described advisors: fleet, telemetry and power documents, not DSU. Uptime Tier: end-of-build certification, not delay probability.
