title: Site-Control Check for Utility Large-Load Queues
one_liner: A neutral 48-hour report on whether each large-load applicant really controls the land it names, sold to the utilities that must now screen speculative data center requests and billed through to the applicants.
customer: Large-load and interconnection managers, plus regulatory counsel, at G&T electric co-ops, municipal utilities and mid-size wires companies. Wedge: Texas co-ops, munis and mid-size TDUs (about 150 entities), then SPP and MISO states. The buyer is the utility. The applicant pays through the study-fee schedule.
problem: Utilities are buried in large-load requests, and many are speculative. The same parcel is shopped to several utilities. 'Site control' is often an applicant-supplied PDF or a non-binding LOI. The utility has to decide which requests get $100k+ studies and reserved capacity. A wrong guess strands capital or pushes cost onto ratepayers. Regulators and commissions now expect screening, but staff have no independent way to check control of land beyond what the applicant says.
solution:
The utility requires the applicant to list its parcels, and we do the rest.
1. Pull recorded instruments on those parcels and their neighbors from county portals, targeted per parcel with a landman fallback, so no bulk licence is needed.
2. Classify by reading the image rather than the clerk's label, and resolve the LLC family by notary, return-to firm and address.
3. Deliver a one-page Site-Control Report graded Recorded, Partial, Unrecorded or Conflicting. It shows acreage under recorded control against the acreage the claimed MW implies, option expiry dates, competing claimants, and duplicate-request flags across utilities through an opt-in hashed-parcel index.
4. Upsell a monthly territory sweep, which is the original Courthouse Tape, for assemblies that have not filed a request yet.
A human landman reviews every Partial or Conflicting result.
why_now: Utilities are being pushed to prove large-load requests are real. Texas SB 6 (2025) reportedly requires 75 MW+ applicants to show site control, disclose duplicate requests and pay study fees. Other utilities have added financial-commitment tariffs. ERCOT's large-load queue is reported at well over 200 GW, far beyond any buildable amount. LLM vision now reads messy recorded instruments accurately. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. Verify the SB 6 details before quoting them to customers.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per Site-Control Report, added as a pass-through line to the applicant's study-fee schedule. $60k-$150k a year per utility for the territory sweep, unlimited reports and a regulator-ready audit pack. Bottom-up: 60 utilities at about $80k is $4.8M ARR in Texas and neighboring states. 500 utilities nationally is about $40M ARR. Later add-on: applicants buy a neutral verified-site-control certificate to speed their queue position.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is much easier than detection. Because the utility can compel the parcel list, we skip the hardest parts of the parent: not knowing where to look, statewide bulk scraping, and false positives. A missing or unrecorded instrument becomes a finding in its own right, which also dodges the doubt that developers may not record option memos before announcement. Only a utility-side neutral can build the moat. Developers shop the same parcel to many utilities, and no utility will share its queue with a vendor that also sells to developers. A cross-utility duplicate-parcel index is therefore a network effect that Enverus or Paces cannot build without losing the trust of their own developer customers.
first_30_days: Take Texas. Call 25 co-op and muni large-load contacts through the Texas Electric Cooperatives and Texas Public Power Association networks and the NRECA circuit. Offer a free retrospective audit of each utility's last 10 requests using only recorded instruments. Report what share had no recorded control, duplicate claims or expired options. Convert two utilities to $20k-$30k paid pilots on new requests. In parallel, confirm which county portals allow per-parcel commercial retrieval and line up two landmen for offline counties.
lineage: mutation of I0773 ('Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: Every competitor in the research sells to developers or investors. Enverus, Paces, GridCARE and DC Byte help a developer find or defend its own site, so utilities cannot treat them as neutral verifiers of a developer's claim. Cleanview and Heatmap Pro start at permit or news, which is after the queue decision. ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds and LLC piercing but not options, leases or easements, and do no per-request verification. Pandell manages a client's own documents. We sell only to the utility side, never to developers, and the audit trail suits a regulator. The remaining risk is Enverus adding the feature, so the cross-utility index and utility trust are the defence.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.

title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.
lineage: mutation of I0428 ('Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte's Demand Package Review is carrier-side workflow (nurse review, 3-10 days, no LOP framing, no signature, no testimony). This is counsel-facing work product, signed and testifiable, and Enlyte reviewers can refer files to us for the signature layer instead of us fighting them for carriers. FAIR Health is a data input and the plaintiff expert's favorite anchor, so the kit pre-rebuts it instead of selling benchmarks. EvenUp is plaintiff-only and its demand packages become our intake format. Turquoise and CLARA sell rate analytics or claims software, not signed opinions. JurisPro-style billing experts are bespoke at $3-5k and slow. We take the repeatable 80% at a tenth of the price and hand the firm an expert only when a file justifies it. Starting in Georgia and Texas avoids Florida's statutory benchmark, and using payer and Medicare anchors avoids the weak hospital-file why-now.

title: Stability Mark: Verified-Stable Tower Registry
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of screening buildings for sinking, certify the many towers that have been stable for 10-30 years with a satellite-verified public mark and lookup registry that agents, lenders and insurers can trust, later backed by a scoping guarantee.
customer: Wedge: boards and building-specialist listing agents at older concrete towers (1970s-2000s) in Aventura, Sunny Isles, Bal Harbour, Brickell and Miami Beach whose owners are stuck with post-Surfside price discounts and need to prove soundness. Second wave: lenders, title companies, master-policy underwriters and MLS platforms as registry API subscribers. Engineers act as co-signers and reviewers.
problem: After Surfside, buyers, lenders and insurers treat every older tower as suspect until proven otherwise. Milestone and SIRS reports are long, alarming to non-engineers and describe conditions, not movement. Florida condo scores like Domexa's or CondoScan's rest on paperwork (did the board file on time?), not on how the ground and structure have behaved. Fine buildings cannot prove they are fine, and unit owners eat a discount. The parent idea also has a demand flaw: boards do not buy reports that might create a discoverable bad document. Selling fear to a reluctant buyer is hard.
solution: The Stability Mark: a 1-page certificate with a QR code to a live registry page, issued only to towers that pass published, pre-registered criteria. Example criteria: at least 10 years of persistent-scatterer coverage (Sentinel-1 alone gives 2016-2026; ERS/Envisat extend it if Miami coverage is usable), no differential settlement above a stated threshold, no accelerating trend, and a matched-control comparison. Participation is opt-in. Passing towers are published. Ambiguous or failing towers get a private result and a monitoring plan, with no public listing. The certificate covers the measurement, not structural safety, and a PE co-signs the method. The method is open and reproducible. There is annual re-verification with automatic revocation triggers, MLS-compatible listing fields, and a lender and insurer API. In year two, add a Scoping Guarantee: a reinsured parametric cover that pays for the Phase 1 engineering evaluation ($15-40K) if a certified tower later trips the threshold, priced at about $150/building/year. The certifier's own capital then stands behind the mark.
why_now: Post-Surfside stigma on older Florida towers is still discounting resale values, and inventory has been elevated since 2024-25 (verify current data). The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines are about to push a wave of alarming paperwork at buyers who cannot interpret it. Reserves can no longer be waived from 2026, so buyers ask about condition. Only satellite archives hold a 1990s-to-present record of how a tower behaved: FIU found Champlain Towers South's 1990s subsidence in ERS data, and no sensor bought today can create that history. Free Sentinel-1 and OPERA data plus NISAR (L-band, from June 2026) make re-verification cheap. Estructura's fear-first marketing leaves the good-news position empty.
revenue_model: Initial certificate $1,800 per building ($995 founding price for the first 50), then $500/year re-verification. PE review fee of about $250 per certificate, and about $60-100 of compute per building. Year two: registry API for lenders, title and insurers at $20K/year flat or $1-3 per lookup, and Scoping Guarantee premium of about $150 per building per year. Year one: about 150 marks at about $1,400 average is roughly $210K, plus $75K recurring. The 10x case: several thousand concrete towers in Florida and tens of thousands nationwide (assumed, verify), with Gulf, Houston, Tampa, Jersey City and Honolulu next. A registry adopted by MLS platforms and lenders, plus a warranty book, is a platform business that a report shop cannot become.
non_obvious_insight: Mandatory-inspection regimes create fear purchases. A voluntary mark creates status purchases, and it has an unraveling dynamic: once 20-30% of comparable towers in a submarket carry the mark, silence becomes a signal that a building is sinking or hiding something, so competitors' badges drive demand rather than the board's fear. Demand rises non-linearly with adoption, which no report business gets. The 10-30 year archive is a cornered resource: nobody can retroactively install a 1996 sensor. Every engineer-reviewed pass or fail adds to a proprietary labeled dataset of which radar signatures precede real findings, which tightens the thresholds and beats sensor bundles that only see the future. The warranty forces honest calibration, since the certifier pays if it is wrong.
first_30_days: Take the parent's roughly 400-tower Sentinel-1 stack and process the 150 oldest concrete towers against the full available archive. Publish the pass criteria before running the results. Confirm persistent-scatterer density and ERS/Envisat usability on Miami; if pre-2015 coverage is poor, use the Sentinel-1 decade. Contract one PE or geodesist to co-sign a methodology memo with measurement-only wording. Approach 10 building-specialist listing agents and 10 presidents of towers that passed, at the $995 founding price. Aim for 8 marks sold, 3 live on agent sites or MLS remarks with the QR code, and 2 lenders or title underwriters willing to read the registry page. Kill test: if fewer than 5 of 20 boards buy at $995, or no PE will co-sign the wording, stop.
lineage: mutation of I1289 ('Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price. | How this version avoids them: Estructura, SmartCore, TRE Altamira, Fugro, Sixense and the other InSAR shops all sell risk detection and monitoring, which is a fear purchase, and none offers a public verified-stable credential. Estructura is also counter-positioned against it: its sensor and AI subscription depends on unseen risk, and a satellite all-clear would cannibalize it, so it cannot rationally copy the mark. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo are paperwork-based scores, paid by buyers at thin price points ($49). The Stability Mark supplies the physical-behavior layer they lack, so Domexa is a distribution partner (they could embed the mark in their scores). OPERA is free but coarse and carries no attestation or per-building certificate. SatSense and Detektia target insurers and engineers abroad. The moat is a published standard, a PE panel, MLS and lender adoption, a labeled dataset and guarantee capital. A copycat has to rebuild all of it.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Cavity ID: Tool-of-Origin Evidence via Counsel
one_liner: Expert-grade 'which tool made this part, and when' reports, built from parts the brand already holds in the US and sold through China-facing IP law firms to brands whose ex-supplier is selling their product.
customer: Wedge: branded hard-goods companies ($10M-$150M revenue: housewares, pet, fitness, hand tools, juvenile, small appliances) that sell injection-molded or die-cast products on Amazon/Walmart/Target, hold a design patent, trade dress or registered mark on the part, and ended a China supplier in the last 18 months. Buyer of record is their outside China/IP counsel (15-25 boutique cross-border firms), who engage us as a consulting expert so the work is privileged. The brand's GC or COO signs off on the disbursement.
problem: The brand sees look-alike units of its own product on Amazon, Temu and 1688 at 30% below its price, and suspects the ex-supplier is running its steel on a third shift. Today its lawyers can send a cease-and-desist built on suspicion, and the supplier answers 'that is a copy, not ours'. Marketplace takedown vendors produce screenshots and listings, not proof of which tool made the part or that it was made after the orders stopped. Without that proof the brand loses the negotiation over tool release, and losing it costs six or seven figures in tooling and margin.
solution: One product, the Tool-of-Origin Report, with no China operations and no extraction business. (1) Baseline: macro-image 30-60 retained parts per SKU, taken from the brand's own US inventory, returns and QA samples across different lots and dates. Build a cavity signature library (cavity ID marks, gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, parting-line and texture flaws) plus a wear-over-time curve, since tool wear is monotonic and dates the tool's state. (2) Attribution: test-buy 5-10 suspect units, match them to a cavity and tool state, and report a forensic-style likelihood ratio, including whether the tool state postdates the last PO. (3) Counsel-ready pack: chain of custody, methodology and a signed declaration from a retained independent molding-process engineer, formatted for the Amazon Report-a-Violation and APEX flows, the Alibaba IP platform, CBP recordation, a demand letter or litigation. Monitoring is bought or white-labeled from an existing vendor. Field capture in China is subcontracted, and only in a later pre-exit 'baseline while the supplier is still cooperative' tier.
why_now: The 2025 tariff whiplash and the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling (per the parent research) have produced a wave of supplier breakups. title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers

title: Community Lenders Pool Orders to Keep County Appraisers
one_liner: Sell rural credit unions and banks a pooled, multi-year county 'appraisal continuity compact', where their combined order flow plus a fixed capacity retainer makes a retiring appraiser's territory viable for a supervised successor.
customer: Payer: the 4-8 community banks and credit unions that originate mortgages in a rural county cluster whose appraiser is retiring, each paying about $3-8k a year, bought through state credit union leagues, bankers associations and their service arms or CUSOs. Beneficiaries: the retiring appraiser (paid a fixed stipend), a mid-career certified appraiser from an adjacent county acting as supervisor, and 1-2 career-changer trainees (agents, inspectors, adjusters).
problem: A rural lender places 30-100 appraisal orders a year. No single small lender can sustain a trainee, and none is big enough to make an out-of-county appraiser drive 60 miles. When the county's only appraiser retires, orders go to distant AMC panel members, closings slip and purchase loans are lost. Trainee programs like Valligent's assume one lender commits volume. The retiree's book was stable because 15 direct lenders each sent about a dozen orders, so each lender was individually too small to replace it.
solution: 'County Compact': (1) Diagnose at-risk counties by joining board rosters (active certified appraisers and license age) with HMDA originations by lender and county. (2) Sign a 3-year compact among 4-8 lenders in the county: pooled first-look on local orders (lenders still order directly and independently, with no link to value conclusions or loan approval), a turnaround SLA such as 7 business days, and a fixed annual capacity retainer paid to us. (3) Recruit and equip the continuity team: a certified supervisor plus 1-2 trainees, with desk QC and UAD 3.6 tooling. (4) Pay the retiree a fixed 12-month knowledge-transfer stipend for the recorded local-knowledge interview, adjustment grids, neighborhood boundary notes and lender introductions. The retiree does not sign reports and gets no percentage of anything. (5) Give each lender a quarterly turnaround and quality report for their compliance and board files. Money flow: borrower pays the appraisal fee through the lender at the customary fee, 100% to the appraiser firm with no skim or split. Lenders pay us the retainer. We pay the retiree a fixed stipend and the supervisor a per-trainee capacity stipend. Counsel to confirm the retainer is independent of order outcomes and that we stay under state AMC registration thresholds (roughly 15 appraisers per state, to verify) because lenders order directly.
why_now: UAD 3.6 goes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and veterans are choosing to quit. ABA Banking Journal and CSBS have documented rural appraiser shortages in 2026. The AQB exposure draft that drops the college-degree requirement widens the trainee pool. EO 14393 signals regulators want more appraiser supply. State leagues and bankers associations already sell shared services to small members, so the channel exists.
revenue_model: Capacity retainer of $3-8k per lender per year scaled by originations, so about $30k a year for a 6-lender compact, on 3-year terms. Add-on lender-paid collateral QC or desk review at roughly $45 per report. 10% distribution share to the league or CUSO. Rough economics (assumptions): year 1 costs are about $10k retiree stipend, $10k supervisor and trainee capacity stipends and $5k ops and QC, leaving a thin margin. Years 2-3 drop the retiree stipend, giving about 45-50% gross margin at steady state. 50 compacts is about $1.5M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Small lenders are each below the minimum viable volume for any successor, but pooled they equal the retiree's book. The compact re-creates that pool contractually. Lenders are not paying for appraisals, which borrowers still cover, but for the option value of local capacity, priced like a rural fire district. A single delayed or lost purchase loan costs a lender more than its share of the retainer, so 2-3 saved closings a year pay for it. Paying supervisors a capacity stipend funded by the pooled retainer solves supervisor scarcity without taking a cut of trainee fees, so fee-splitting rules are avoided.
first_30_days: Build a county risk map for TX, OH, PA and CO from board rosters and HMDA and NCUA/FFIEC lender lists, and shortlist 15 counties with an aging appraiser and 4+ community lenders. Call appraisal or ordering managers at 20 credit unions and banks and ask which orders were delayed or unplaceable in the last 12 months and what each cost. Offer two state leagues or bankers associations free county risk maps for their members as the door-opener and ask for a pilot. Recruit 2 supervisors and 4 trainees. Get a signed letter of intent for 2 pilot compacts of 3+ lenders each. Commission one counsel memo on appraisal independence and AMC thresholds.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. (2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.

(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.

Solidifi and AXIS are AMC mentor-matching programs, while this is lender-funded capacity in named counties. PAREA gives experience without supervisors but transfers no local knowledge and does not guarantee anyone orders. title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
